chapters.title: PESTLE & the External Business Environment
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: A government announces a sustained programme of higher public spending and also signals that it will maintain strict control of public finances. Which PESTLE category is most directly concerned with these developments?
questions.explanation: Government spending and fiscal policy are classified as Political in this PESTLE teaching framework; they also have economic effects.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 1; Notion sample-bank reference: 1.

questions.stem: An SME completes a PESTLE analysis and concludes that it has a strong internal capability to exploit a new market. Why should this conclusion not be treated as a PESTLE finding by itself?

options.text: PESTLE focuses on the external environment and does not assess internal strengths, weaknesses or capabilities
PESTLE is designed only to analyse financial statements
PESTLE cannot be used for strategic planning

questions.explanation: PESTLE examines external conditions. Internal capabilities belong in an internal analysis such as SWOT.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 2; Notion sample-bank reference: 2.

questions.stem: A bakery’s customers have experienced rising prices for many goods. The bakery is concerned that, even where nominal household incomes rise, customers may have less purchasing power. Which PESTLE factor is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Real income measures purchasing power after allowing for changes in prices.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 3; Notion sample-bank reference: 3.

questions.stem: An Irish business is considering selling more products in the UK. The euro falls in value relative to sterling. What is the most direct effect of this currency depreciation on goods imported from the UK into Ireland?
questions.explanation: A weaker euro buys fewer pounds, raising the euro cost of UK imports, other things equal.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 4; Notion sample-bank reference: 4.

questions.stem: An SME bakery finds that changes in the age structure of the population are altering demand for different types of baked goods. Which PESTLE category does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Age structure and demographics are Social factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 5; Notion sample-bank reference: 5.

questions.stem: A bakery introduces automated production equipment and robotics to speed up its production process and reduce costs. Which PESTLE category best captures this development?
questions.explanation: Automation and robotics fall under Technological factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 6; Notion sample-bank reference: 6.

questions.stem: A company must change how it stores and processes customers’ personal information because of the GDPR. Which PESTLE category should this issue be placed under?
questions.explanation: Data-protection obligations are Legal factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 7; Notion sample-bank reference: 7.

questions.stem: A business is assessing how climate change, carbon-reduction pressures and the transition to lower-emission operations could affect its costs and long-term plans. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: Climate and sustainability pressures are Environmental factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 8; Notion sample-bank reference: 8.

questions.stem: A manager uses PESTLE analysis to identify an emerging external threat before it has a serious effect on the business. Which advantage of PESTLE is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: PESTLE can identify external risks early.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 9; Notion sample-bank reference: 9.

questions.stem: An Irish SME bakery is considering expanding into the UK. The management team is particularly concerned that changes in the euro–sterling exchange rate could alter the cost of ingredients and other imported inputs. Which PESTLE factor should it examine most directly?
questions.explanation: Exchange-rate movements are Economic factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 11; Notion sample-bank reference: 11.

questions.stem: An SME wants to improve its green credentials and asks managers to use PESTLE analysis. The team produces a long list of climate, carbon-pricing and sustainability issues but cannot decide which ones should influence its strategy. Which disadvantage of PESTLE is most clearly illustrated?
questions.explanation: An unprioritised list prevents decisions: analysis paralysis.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 12; Notion sample-bank reference: 12.

questions.stem: An Irish bakery is researching whether demand in the UK may differ from demand in Ireland because of differences in customer tastes, culture and demographic patterns. Which PESTLE category is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Culture, preferences and demographics are Social factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 13; Notion sample-bank reference: 13.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is considering moving some operations from Cork to Poland. Before making the investment, managers want to assess how regulation and employment-law requirements, including statutory minimum-wage rules, could affect the operation. Which PESTLE category is this?
questions.explanation: Regulation, employment law and statutory wage requirements are Legal factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 14; Notion sample-bank reference: 14.

questions.stem: An IT company is considering a major new investment in Ireland. Its managers want to understand how rapid developments in AI, digitalisation, payment systems and cybersecurity could affect the competitiveness of the investment. Which PESTLE category should they focus on?
questions.explanation: AI, digitalisation and cybersecurity are Technological factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 16; Notion sample-bank reference: 16.

questions.stem: An indigenous small IT company is considering expanding its product range. The owners believe that technological innovation could allow it to develop new products and increase the added value offered to customers. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant to this external opportunity?
questions.explanation: Technological innovation can create external product-development opportunities.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 18; Notion sample-bank reference: 18.

questions.stem: An SME agri-business is considering moving manufacturing to China. Its board wants to assess the possible impact of tariffs, trade policy and geopolitical risk on the proposed move. Which PESTLE category should be used?
questions.explanation: Tariffs, trade policy and geopolitical risk are Political factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 19; Notion sample-bank reference: 19.

questions.stem: An agri-business is also considering how access to raw materials and longer-term sustainability issues could affect the proposed manufacturing strategy. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: Natural-resource availability and sustainability are Environmental factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 20; Notion sample-bank reference: 20.

questions.stem: A Cork medical-device exporter faces a new EU product-certification rule and a simultaneous fall in sterling. Which analysis best separates the two developments?

options.text: Certification is a legal factor; sterling depreciation is an economic factor that may reduce euro receipts from UK sales.
Certification is technological; sterling depreciation necessarily increases euro receipts.
Certification is social; exchange-rate changes cannot affect competitiveness.
Both are political factors, because governments influence each.

questions.explanation: Product-certification requirements are legal constraints. A weaker pound can reduce the euro value of unchanged sterling receipts, so the exchange-rate change is economic.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q1; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q1.

questions.stem: A PESTLE exercise produces such a long list of possible external developments that managers cannot decide which issues to act on. Which disadvantage of PESTLE does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Too many findings without priorities can produce analysis paralysis.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 10; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: 10.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company considering moving operations from Cork to Poland is also assessing the risks associated with political stability, geopolitical developments and trade policy in the countries connected to its new supply chain. Which PESTLE category captures these issues?
questions.explanation: Political stability, geopolitical risk and trade policy are Political factors.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 15; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: 15.

questions.stem: An IT company is deciding whether to increase its investment in Ireland. One part of its external-environment assessment considers government spending, corporate and personal tax, fiscal risks and political stability. Which PESTLE category does this describe?
questions.explanation: Tax policy, government spending and political stability are Political in the lecture framework.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 17; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: 17.

chapters.title: Shareholder Wealth, Present Value & Profit
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines shareholder wealth?

options.text: The firm's total accounting profit in the current year
The present value of expected future cash returns to equity owners
The total value of the firm's outstanding bonds
The value of the firm's physical assets before liabilities

questions.explanation: Shareholder wealth concerns the value of expected future returns to equity owners.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 21; Notion sample-bank reference: 21.

questions.stem: Which formula correctly calculates the present value of a single future sum?
questions.explanation: Divide the future sum by its compound discount factor.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 25; Notion sample-bank reference: 25.

questions.stem: Holding the future cash flow and time period constant, what happens when the discount rate rises?

options.text: Present value becomes equal to future value

questions.explanation: A larger discount denominator lowers present value for an unchanged positive cash flow.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 27; Notion sample-bank reference: 27.

questions.stem: A firm reports a positive accounting profit, but the return is below what the owner could earn from the next-best alternative. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: The project necessarily maximises shareholder wealth
Economic profit may be negative because opportunity cost is not covered
Opportunity cost is irrelevant once accounting profit is positive

questions.explanation: Implicit opportunity costs can exceed the positive accounting profit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 33; Notion sample-bank reference: 33.

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate when calculating the present value of several annual cash flows?

options.text: Add the undiscounted cash flows and discount the total once using Year 1
Discount each cash flow for its own time period and then add the present values
Use the risk-free rate even when a required return is supplied
Round every intermediate step to the nearest whole euro

questions.explanation: Discount each cash flow for the time until it is received, then sum.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 29; Notion sample-bank reference: 29.

questions.stem: Why is shareholder wealth maximisation broader than simple profit maximisation?

options.text: It ignores risk but includes tax
It focuses only on the largest annual profit
It accounts for the timing and risk of expected future returns
It treats all stakeholders as equity owners

questions.explanation: Timing and risk matter as well as the amount of returns.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 22; Notion sample-bank reference: 22.

questions.stem: Which is not itself a reason to discount future money?
questions.explanation: Market share is not itself a reason to discount money.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 23; Notion sample-bank reference: 23.

questions.stem: An investor requires a higher return from an oil-exploration project than from a safe deposit. Which concept best explains the difference?
questions.explanation: Additional investment risk can require a risk premium.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 24; Notion sample-bank reference: 24.

questions.stem: What is the approximate present value of €110 received in one year when the discount rate is 10%?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 26; Notion sample-bank reference: 26.

questions.stem: A share has expected returns of €5, €6 and €7 at the ends of Years 1, 2 and 3. At a 10% discount rate, what is their approximate total present value?
questions.explanation: €5/1.10 = €4.545455; €6/1.10² = €4.958678; €7/1.10³ = €5.259204. Add before rounding: €14.763336 ≈ €14.76. The earlier €14.77 used rounded intermediate values.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 28; Notion sample-bank reference: 28.

questions.stem: A project has an NPV of −€4,500. What decision follows from the standard NPV rule?

options.text: Accept because all cash inflows are positive
Accept because the initial investment is already paid
Reject because the project destroys value relative to the required return

questions.explanation: Negative NPV fails the required return, so reject under the standard rule.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 31; Notion sample-bank reference: 31.

questions.stem: Let VC denote variable cost per unit and FC total fixed cost. Which set of identities is correct?
questions.explanation: Profit = revenue − cost; revenue = price × quantity; total cost = unit variable cost × quantity + fixed cost. Here VC means variable cost per unit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 32; Notion sample-bank reference: 32.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes real and nominal required rates of return?

options.text: Real required returns are determined by inflation alone
A real required return reflects opportunity cost, time preference and risk; a nominal required return also allows for expected inflation
Nominal required returns must equal the risk-free rate
Real required returns automatically fall as investment risk rises

questions.explanation: A real required return reflects opportunity cost, time preference and risk. A nominal required return also allows for expected inflation; cash flows and rates must use consistent nominal or real terms.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 34; Notion sample-bank reference: 34.

questions.stem: Which management decision would most directly increase shareholder value, all else equal?

options.text: Increasing expected costs without changing revenue
Delaying the same cash flow while keeping risk unchanged
Increasing expected future cash returns without increasing the required return
Raising the discount rate applied to unchanged cash flows

questions.explanation: Larger expected returns at the same required return increase present value.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 35; Notion sample-bank reference: 35.

questions.stem: A firm expects profits per share of €4, €5 and €6 in Years 1–3. Investors require a return of 10%. What is the present value of one share?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 36; Notion sample-bank reference: 36.

questions.stem: A company expects profits per share of €8, €9 and €10 in Years 1–3. The required return is 8%. What is the present value of one share?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 37; Notion sample-bank reference: 37.

questions.stem: Holding expected future profits constant, what is the effect of an increase in investors’ required rate of return on the current value of a share?

options.text: It first increases and then reduces the share value

questions.explanation: A higher required return lowers the present value of unchanged positive future profits.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 38; Notion sample-bank reference: 38.

questions.stem: A firm sells 2,000 units at €25 per unit. What is total revenue?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 39; Notion sample-bank reference: 39.

questions.stem: A firm’s total revenue is €120,000 and it sells 4,000 units. What is the price per unit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 40; Notion sample-bank reference: 40.

questions.stem: A firm produces 5,000 units, has a variable cost of €12 per unit and fixed costs of €20,000. What is total cost?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 41; Notion sample-bank reference: 41.

questions.stem: A firm sells 10,000 units at €30 each. Variable cost is €18 per unit and fixed costs are €60,000. What is profit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 42; Notion sample-bank reference: 42.

questions.stem: A firm sells at €40 per unit, has a variable cost of €25 per unit and fixed costs of €50,000. What is profit at an output of 6,000 units?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 43; Notion sample-bank reference: 43.

questions.stem: A firm’s price is €50, variable cost is €30 per unit and fixed costs are €100,000. What output gives zero profit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 44; Notion sample-bank reference: 44.

questions.stem: A project costs €1,000 today and pays €660 at the end of each of Years 1 and 2. There are no other cash flows. At a 10% required return, what are its NPV and the standard investment decision?
questions.explanation: NPV = −€1,000 + €660/1.10 + €660/1.10² = €145.45 after rounding. The positive NPV supports acceptance under the standard rule.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M2.

questions.stem: You invest €800 for three years at 5% interest compounded annually, with no withdrawals. What is the future value, rounded to cents?
questions.explanation: FV = €800 × 1.05³ = €926.10. €920 uses simple interest rather than annual compounding.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M3.

questions.stem: A firm charges €35 per unit, incurs €21 variable cost per unit and has €42,000 fixed costs. Assuming every unit produced is sold, what output gives zero profit?
questions.explanation: Contribution per unit is €35 − €21 = €14. Break-even output is €42,000/€14 = 3,000 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #2 — PV, FV, NPV and profit; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M4.

questions.stem: An Irish SME pays €100,000 today for a machine generating €60,000 at the end of each of the next two years, with no scrap value. At a 10% discount rate, which conclusion is closest?

options.text: NPV is approximately +€9,091, because only year two is discounted.
NPV is +€20,000, because discounting is irrelevant over two years.
NPV is approximately +€4,132; accept if risk and other assumptions are adequately reflected.

questions.explanation: NPV = −100,000 + 60,000/1.10 + 60,000/(1.10²) = +€4,132.23. A positive NPV supports acceptance when the discount rate and cash-flow assumptions adequately reflect risk.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q2; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q2.

questions.stem: What does a positive NPV indicate?

options.text: The project fails to recover its initial cost in present-value terms
The project exactly earns the required return
The project adds value after allowing for the required return
The project's accounting profit must be zero

questions.explanation: Positive NPV means value is added above the required return.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 30; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: 30.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the shareholder wealth-maximisation model?

options.text: Shareholder wealth is determined only by the firm’s fixed costs
The objective is to maximise sales regardless of costs
Shareholder wealth is related to the present value of expected future cash returns
The objective is to maximise current-period accounting profit only

questions.explanation: Shareholder value is linked to discounted expected future cash returns.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 45; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: 45.

questions.stem: An investment pays €1,210 at the end of Year 2 and nothing else. At a 10% annual discount rate, what is its present value?
questions.explanation: PV = €1,210/(1.10)^2 = €1,000. The single payment is discounted for two years.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question M1; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: M1.

chapters.title: Markets, Economic Systems & Price Signals
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: Hardware shops charge higher prices for snow shovels after a big snowstorm. What role do prices play in the snow-shovel market?

options.text: In an emergency, prices must remain fixed; therefore, prices do not play a role in this case
Higher prices incentivise distributors to ship more snow shovels into the area to meet the increased demand
Prices signal when price gouging is taking place so authorities can step in to prevent it
In such a natural disaster, prices do not efficiently guide the invisible hand

questions.explanation: Higher prices encourage suppliers to direct additional stock towards increased demand.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 46; Notion sample-bank reference: 46.

questions.stem: In the introductory competitive-market model without relevant market failures, how do price signals support coordination?

options.text: They convey information and align incentives, helping self-interested decisions direct resources towards valued uses
They eliminate the need for firms to respond to consumer preferences
They provide information but cannot influence production incentives
They require a central authority to determine every household purchase

questions.explanation: All three statements describe price signals within the competitive-market framework; this depends on the absence of relevant market failures.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 47; Notion sample-bank reference: 47.

questions.stem: Commuters in Beijing find it difficult to get a cab at rush hour while hundreds of cabs lie idle outside cab companies. Demand and fuel prices have risen, but the government has left the base fare unchanged. What government action is likely to correct the situation?

options.text: Lift the price control on the base fare for cabs
Restrict the entry of new cabs

questions.explanation: Removing the binding fare control allows price to adjust to demand and supply conditions.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 48; Notion sample-bank reference: 48.

questions.stem: How do profits and losses allocate resources in a market economy?

options.text: Profits attract resources and entry to valued products; losses encourage reallocation or exit
Profits prevent new entry while losses require firms to expand
Profits and losses have no influence on investment decisions
Losses attract resources because they demonstrate high unmet profitability

questions.explanation: Profits attract resources and entry; losses encourage reallocation or exit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 49; Notion sample-bank reference: 49.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of the market economy?

options.text: It generates lower economic output than a command economy
It aligns incentives but fails to coordinate economic agents
It inherently facilitates coordination between economic agents and aligns incentives
It facilitates coordination between economic agents but misaligns incentives

questions.explanation: Prices help coordinate decentralised decisions and align incentives in the market model.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 50; Notion sample-bank reference: 50.

questions.stem: The concept of the invisible hand was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Adam Smith introduced the invisible-hand concept.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 51; Notion sample-bank reference: 51.

questions.stem: Which outcome describes the intended benefits of the invisible hand in the introductory competitive-market model?

options.text: Competition can encourage efficient methods, improved products and lower prices
Self-interest guarantees efficient outcomes even with externalities or monopoly power
Competition removes any incentive to improve products
Self-interest ensures every firm earns permanent economic profit

questions.explanation: These are the intended competitive-market benefits in the introductory model, not guarantees for every market.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 52; Notion sample-bank reference: 52.

questions.stem: The concept of the invisible hand refers to:

options.text: A central authority allocating every productive resource
Individuals making decisions in their own self-interest
The Federal Reserve setting interest rates

questions.explanation: Decentralised self-interested decisions can coordinate through prices.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 53; Notion sample-bank reference: 53.

questions.stem: The concept of self-interest, as understood in the invisible-hand model, refers to:
questions.explanation: Self-regarding means pursuing one’s own objectives or welfare; it does not require selfishness.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 54; Notion sample-bank reference: 54.

questions.stem: A sudden shortage of cocoa raises its price. A confectionery firm switches to recipes using less cocoa without learning why the shortage arose. Which interpretation most closely reflects Hayek’s argument?

options.text: Only a central authority can coordinate a response to the shortage.
Price signals remove scarcity rather than changing responses to it.
Prices communicate dispersed information and induce economising without every decision-maker knowing the underlying cause.
A higher cocoa price proves that demand must have increased.

questions.explanation: Hayek’s price-system argument is that prices communicate dispersed information. The higher cocoa price encourages economising even when firms do not know the cause of scarcity.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q3; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q3.

questions.stem: A profitable market attracts new independent suppliers over time. Assuming demand and input costs do not change, which sequence is most consistent with competition and Smith’s market coordination?

options.text: Market supply shifts left, price rises, and profits necessarily increase indefinitely.
Individual firms gain permanent pricing power simply because more firms enter.
Market supply shifts right, equilibrium price falls, and above-normal economic profits tend to be competed away.
Demand shifts right, price rises, and entry is discouraged.

questions.explanation: With demand and input costs unchanged, entry increases market supply. Equilibrium price falls and competitive pressure tends to erode above-normal economic profits.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q4; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q4.

chapters.title: Demand, Supply & Curve Shifts
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the major factors that shifts the demand curve when it changes?

options.text: The price of the good itself

questions.explanation: A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along its demand curve.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 66; Notion sample-bank reference: 66.

questions.stem: There are five students who are looking to buy one second-hand textbook each. Their willingness to pay is £5, £6, £8, £12 and £15, respectively. Which statement is correct?

options.text: To sell three books, the maximum price that can be charged is £8.
The student with a willingness to pay of £15 is the richest.
If a seller is one of many identical sellers and his reservation price is £8, then he is guaranteed to sell his textbook.
Their willingness to pay indicates an upward-sloping demand curve.

questions.explanation: At £8, three students are willing to buy; above £8, only two are. Willingness to pay does not reveal wealth or guarantee a sale.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 60; Notion sample-bank reference: 60.

questions.stem: A poor wheat harvest occurred in 1845. Average prices in 1838–45 → maximum prices in 1845–48 (relative to silver) were: Austria 52.9 → 104.0 and Hungary 39.0 → 92.3, both with violent revolution in 1848; England 115.3 → 134.7 and Sweden 75.8 → 81.4, both without violent revolution. Which statement is supported?

options.text: A downward shift of the supply curve caused the price hike.
A high average price of wheat caused violent revolution.
Countries with a violent revolution necessarily had a more inelastic demand curve.
There is a positive correlation between large wheat-price hikes and the incidence of violent revolution.

questions.explanation: The price changes are about 96.6%, 136.7%, 16.8% and 7.4%, respectively. The data support an association, not proof of causation or demand elasticity.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 63; Notion sample-bank reference: 63.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the major factors that shifts the supply curve when it changes?

options.text: Prices of inputs used in production

questions.explanation: Consumer income shifts demand. Input costs, seller numbers and relevant expectations can shift supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 64; Notion sample-bank reference: 64.

questions.stem: The wine industry relies on unskilled labour to pick grapes. Other things equal, an increase in immigration that increases the available labour supply and reduces labour costs will shift the supply curve of wine:

options.text: The supply curve becomes perfectly vertical

questions.explanation: Lower labour costs make more wine profitable to supply at each price. The cost assumption makes the original question explicit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 65; Notion sample-bank reference: 65.

questions.stem: Which factor is expected to cause the demand curve for coffee to shift to the right?

options.text: A higher tax on the sale of tea, a substitute for coffee
A fall in the manufacturing cost of coffee
A higher personal tax on the income of all consumers
An increase in the supply of coffee due to better weather

questions.explanation: A tax that raises the price of tea encourages substitution towards coffee. Coffee production costs and weather affect coffee supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 68; Notion sample-bank reference: 68.

questions.stem: Quinoa production and prices rose following stronger overseas demand. With other factors held constant, which interpretation fits the demand-and-supply model?

options.text: Demand shifted right, and higher prices encourage other countries to increase production
Supply shifted left, and the resulting higher price benefits every buyer
Demand shifted left, and higher prices discourage production elsewhere
Demand shifted right, and the higher price necessarily benefits everyone in producing countries

questions.explanation: Higher demand explains the joint rise in price and output. Higher prices encourage additional production but hurt buyers. The charts are summarised by their relevant trend, and the demand-shift interpretation is conditional on other factors being unchanged. Source charts
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 71; Notion sample-bank reference: 71.

questions.stem: New technology shifts the bread supply curve right/down, while demand and the number of bakeries remain unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakeries’ marginal cost of production has fallen.
Excess demand at the original price has led to the fall in equilibrium price.
The more elastic the demand curve, the larger the fall in price.
There has been an increase in demand.

questions.explanation: The technology reduces costs. At the old price there is excess supply. The stated shift makes the diagram-based question self-contained.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 72; Notion sample-bank reference: 72.

questions.stem: A fall in the price of a substitute raises demand for the substitute and reduces demand for takeaway pizza. At the same time, higher energy costs reduce pizza supply. Which outcome can be predicted with certainty?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises and quantity rises.
Equilibrium quantity of pizza falls; the direction of the price change is ambiguous.
Both equilibrium price and quantity necessarily fall.
Equilibrium price falls and quantity rises.

questions.explanation: The fall in pizza demand and the fall in pizza supply both reduce equilibrium quantity. The demand change puts downward pressure on price, while the supply change puts upward pressure on it, so the net price effect is ambiguous.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q7; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q7.

chapters.title: Market Equilibrium, Shortages & Surpluses
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: In a standard competitive model without externalities, demand shifts right/up as consumers become richer and supply shifts right/down as marginal costs fall. What follows?

options.text: Quantity traded and total surplus rise; the direction of the price change is indeterminate
Price must fall, while quantity traded must fall
Price must rise, while total surplus must fall
Quantity traded stays constant, while price must fall

questions.explanation: Price depends on the relative shifts. Both changes increase traded quantity. Higher willingness to pay and lower production costs increase the gains from trade in this model.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 73; Notion sample-bank reference: 73.

questions.stem: Z is a normal good. Its equilibrium price and quantity were €25 and 60 units in 2020. In 2021 they increased to €35 and 70 units. Other things equal, which change could explain this?

options.text: A shift of demand for Z to the right
A shift of demand for Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the right
A shift of supply of Z to the left

questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises both equilibrium price and quantity with unchanged upward-sloping supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 69; Notion sample-bank reference: 69.

questions.stem: Z is a normal good. Its equilibrium price and quantity were €25 and 60 units in 2020. In 2021 they decreased to €15 and 50 units. Other things equal, which change could explain this?

options.text: A shift of demand for Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the right
A shift of demand for Z to the right

questions.explanation: A leftward demand shift lowers both price and quantity with unchanged supply.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 70; Notion sample-bank reference: 70.

questions.stem: The textbook market has demand P = 20 − 0.5Q and supply P = 2 + 0.25Q, with price in dollars. Which statement is correct?

options.text: At a price of $6, there is excess demand of 4 books.
There are sellers willing to give away their textbooks for free.
At a price of $12, all books offered for sale will be sold.

questions.explanation: 20 − 0.5Q = 2 + 0.25Q gives Q = 24 and P = 8. At 6, Qd = 28 and Qs = 16, so excess demand is 12 books. The replacement uses the matching CORE textbook-market model. Source model
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 62; Notion sample-bank reference: 62.

questions.stem: National income increases by 20%, causing a 20% increase in houses demanded at every price. Assume demand slopes downward and the unchanged supply curve slopes upward with finite elasticity. The equilibrium number of houses traded is likely to:
questions.explanation: The demand shift raises price; this reduces part of the quantity increase. Perfectly elastic supply would instead allow a 20% increase; perfectly inelastic supply would leave quantity unchanged. The original omitted the supply assumption.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 67; Notion sample-bank reference: 67.

questions.stem: More students arrive, shifting textbook demand right/up while an upward-sloping supply curve remains unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Every buyer who would have bought before the shift will still buy after it.
The more inelastic supply is, the larger the increase in quantity traded.
There has been an increase in supply.
The more elastic supply is, the smaller the price rise.

questions.explanation: Supply elasticity governs how much adjustment occurs through quantity rather than price.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 85; Notion sample-bank reference: 85.

questions.stem: A competitive market has demand P=30−0.2Q. Supply changes from S₀: P=0.1Q to S₁: P=6+0.1Q, while demand is unchanged. Using the diagram and equations, what are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Equate demand with the replacement supply: 30−0.2Q=6+0.1Q. Thus Q=80 and P=€14. The original equilibrium was Q=100 and P=€10.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, Section P2; latest lecture-based practice variation. Numerical models and diagrams are illustrative, not lecturer measurements.; Notion sample-bank reference: P2.

questions.stem: Demand is Qd=150−5P and supply is Qs=30+3P, where P is euros per unit. Which equilibrium pair is correct?
questions.explanation: Set 150−5P=30+3P: 120=8P, so P=€15. Both schedules give Q=75.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #3 — equilibrium algebra and adjustment; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M6.

questions.stem: A market has demand Qd=150−5P and supply Qs=30+3P. If price is held at €10, what is the market imbalance?
questions.explanation: At P=10, Qd=100 and Qs=60. The shortage is Qd−Qs=40 units.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #3 — equilibrium algebra and adjustment; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M7.

questions.stem: Supply is Qs=30+3P. Demand changes from Qd=150−5P to Qd=190−5P, with price in euros per unit. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Use the new demand schedule: 190−5P=30+3P, so P=20 and Q=90. The rightward demand shift raises both equilibrium values.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #3 — equilibrium algebra and adjustment; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M8.

questions.stem: Aldi estimates demand Qd = 150 − 3P and supply Qs = 30 + 2P for a wine. A €5 per-bottle tax on suppliers changes supply to Qs = 30 + 2(P − 5). What are the new consumer price and equilibrium quantity?
questions.explanation: After the tax, Qs = 30 + 2(P − 5) = 20 + 2P. Equating supply and demand gives 150 − 3P = 20 + 2P, hence P = €26 and Q = 72. P is the consumer price; suppliers receive €21 after tax.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q5; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q5.

questions.stem: In the figure, both demand and supply shift vertically upwards by €12 at every quantity (D0→D1 and S0→S1). What happens to equilibrium?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises while equilibrium quantity remains unchanged.
Equilibrium quantity rises while price is unchanged.
Both price and quantity are unchanged.

questions.explanation: Raising both inverse demand and inverse supply by the same €12 leaves their intersection’s quantity unchanged and raises its price by €12. In the chart, Q remains 24 while P rises from €31.20 to €43.20.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q6; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q6.

image.alt: Price (€) against quantity, with downward-sloping D0 and D1 and upward-sloping S0 and S1; D1 and S1 lie €12 above their corresponding original curves.

questions.stem: A market has Qd = 120 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 30. The government imposes a binding maximum price of €24. What shortage results?
questions.explanation: At the maximum price of €24, Qd = 120 − 2(24) = 72 and Qs = 3(24) − 30 = 42. The shortage is 72 − 42 = 30 units.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q8; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q8.

questions.stem: Cost-saving inventions make paint cheaper to produce, while longer-lasting paint means buildings need repainting less often. With other factors unchanged, what can be predicted?

options.text: Price falls; the change in quantity is ambiguous.
Price is ambiguous; quantity necessarily falls.
Both price and quantity necessarily rise.

questions.explanation: Cost-saving technology shifts supply right, while less frequent repainting shifts demand left. Both changes lower equilibrium price; their effects on quantity oppose one another.
questions.source: OS1; adapted from OpenStax, Chapter 3, self-check 3 — https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/3-self-check-questions. Principles of Economics 3e, Steven A. questions.stem: Hailstorms increase the need to repaint buildings and simultaneously force several paint factories to close. Which equilibrium result is certain in the standard model?

options.text: Price rises, while quantity may rise or fall.
Quantity rises, while price may rise or fall.
Quantity and price both stay unchanged.

questions.explanation: Repainting needs shift demand right and factory closures shift supply left. Both raise equilibrium price, while their opposing quantity effects leave the quantity change uncertain.
questions.source: OS2; adapted from OpenStax, Chapter 3, self-check 3 — https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/3-self-check-questions. Principles of Economics 3e, Steven A. questions.stem: Cars become more fuel-efficient, reducing oil needed per kilometre. Holding driving and all other conditions constant, what happens in the oil market?

options.text: Demand shifts left; equilibrium price and quantity fall.
The oil demand curve does not shift; only a movement along it occurs.

questions.explanation: With driving held constant, greater fuel efficiency reduces oil demand at every price. A leftward demand shift lowers equilibrium price and quantity, other things equal.
questions.source: OS3; adapted from OpenStax, Chapter 3, self-check 4 — https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/3-self-check-questions. Principles of Economics 3e, Steven A. questions.stem: Jet fuel becomes more expensive for airlines. With demand for flights unchanged and upward-sloping supply, what is the expected effect?

options.text: Flight supply shifts right; fares fall.
Flight demand shifts left; fares fall.
Flight demand shifts right; fares rise.
Flight supply shifts left; fares rise and the quantity of flights falls.

questions.explanation: Higher jet-fuel costs reduce the supply of flights. With demand unchanged, the leftward supply shift raises fares and reduces the equilibrium quantity of flights.

chapters.title: Allocation, Surplus & Limits of Markets
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: Mary is willing to pay at most €40 for a bracelet. She buys it for €22.50. What consumer surplus does she gain?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price = €40 − €22.50 = €17.50.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 78; Notion sample-bank reference: 78.

questions.stem: For straight-line bread demand and supply curves, keep their intersection (equilibrium price and output) unchanged while varying slopes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A less elastic demand curve leads to smaller consumer surplus.
A less elastic supply curve leads to larger producer surplus.
A more elastic demand curve leads to smaller producer surplus when supply is unchanged.
Consumer and producer surplus do not depend on curve elasticities.

questions.explanation: Steeper supply increases the area between price and supply to the left of equilibrium. The linear-curve assumption makes the original diagram-based comparison precise.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 86; Notion sample-bank reference: 86.

questions.stem: The figure shows a competitive market. At the equilibrium, what is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: The graph shows equilibrium at Q = 20 and P = €40, with a demand-price intercept of €80. Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 20 × (€80 − €40) = €400.

chapters.title: Consumers — Marginal Utility & Demand Elasticities
chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: At an interior optimum with diminishing marginal benefits, a consumer’s satisfaction is maximised when marginal benefit per euro is equal across goods because:

options.text: Any small reallocation of expenditure towards either good would fail to improve satisfaction.
Any shift in consumption towards either good violates the budget constraint.
Her preferences become invalid when marginal benefits per euro differ.
Unequal ratios imply that she has insufficient income to maximise satisfaction.

questions.explanation: If one good yielded more benefit per euro, shifting spending towards it would improve satisfaction. The interior-optimum assumption avoids corner-solution exceptions.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 76; Notion sample-bank reference: 76.

questions.stem: Holding other forces constant, a rise in motor-fuel prices produces a larger fall in quantity demanded over ten years than immediately because:

options.text: Buyers are more sensitive to price changes when given more time to respond.
Long-run demand is perfectly inelastic because consumers have more time to adjust
Buyers are less sensitive to price changes when given more time to react.
Buyers necessarily have substantially more income after ten years.

questions.explanation: People have more time to change vehicles, travel habits or location, making long-run demand more elastic.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 83; Notion sample-bank reference: 83.

questions.stem: A restaurant increases its pizza price from €12 to €15. Sales fall from 200 to 160 pizzas per week. Using initial values as the percentage-change base, what is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Quantity change: (160 − 200)/200 = −20%. Price change: (15 − 12)/12 = 25%. PED = −20/25 = −0.8. Using the midpoint method instead gives −1.0; the method must be specified.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 74; Notion sample-bank reference: 74.

questions.stem: A drought reduces the available quantity of wheat by 20%. If PED is −0.5, use the percentage-change elasticity approximation to estimate the price increase needed for quantity demanded to fall by 20%.
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = PED × %ΔP, so %ΔP = −20%/−0.5 = 40%. This is the introductory approximation, not an exact large-change prediction from a constant-elasticity demand function.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 75; Notion sample-bank reference: 75.

questions.stem: Total expected extra marks from studying for 1–5 hours are 10, 14, 18, 21 and 23; total marks lost through tiredness are 0, 3, 7, 12 and 18. Which pair of durations ties for the highest net expected marks?
questions.explanation: Net benefits: 1 hour = 10 − 0 = 10; 2 = 14 − 3 = 11; 3 = 18 − 7 = 11; 4 = 21 − 12 = 9; 5 = 23 − 18 = 5. Both 2 and 3 hours maximise net marks. The third hour has MB = MC = 4, so it adds zero net benefit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 77; Notion sample-bank reference: 77.

questions.stem: The price of bags rises from €11 to €13 and quantity demanded falls from 56 to 52. A further table row gives €15 and 44 bags. Using the initial point (€11, 56) and the €11 → €13 interval, what is the absolute price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: ΔQ = −4 and ΔP = 2. Initial-point estimate: (−4/2) × (11/56) = −0.392857, absolute value ≈ 0.39. The midpoint/arc value is about 0.44, which was incorrectly mixed into the original point-elasticity question.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 79; Notion sample-bank reference: 79.

questions.stem: Last year John bought 50 pounds of mincemeat when household income was €40,000. This year income was €30,000 and he bought 60 pounds. All else constant, his income elasticity is:

options.text: Negative, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Negative, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.

questions.explanation: Quantity rises as income falls. Using initial values gives (10/50)/(−10,000/40,000) = −0.8.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 80; Notion sample-bank reference: 80.

questions.stem: In any market where units sell at a common price, total revenue is price:

options.text: Divided by the price elasticity of demand
Multiplied by quantity minus production costs

questions.explanation: TR = P × Q. Subtracting costs gives profit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 81; Notion sample-bank reference: 81.

questions.stem: The cross-price elasticity of food demand with respect to the price of entertainment is −0.7. If entertainment prices rise by 20%, the percentage-change approximation predicts that food quantity demanded:

options.text: Rises by 0.14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are complements.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 0.14%, and the goods are complements.

questions.explanation: %ΔQfood = −0.7 × 20% = −14%. A negative cross-price elasticity identifies complements.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 82; Notion sample-bank reference: 82.

questions.stem: You and your housemate each eat three packets of Pot Noodles weekly. After your incomes rise, you buy more while your housemate buys fewer and substitutes preferred foods. Your income elasticity and your housemate’s are, respectively:
questions.explanation: The same product can be normal for one person and inferior for another.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 84; Notion sample-bank reference: 84.

questions.stem: Use the table of product Y’s price and product X’s quantity demanded. Other influences are held constant. Using initial-value percentage changes, what is X’s cross-price elasticity with respect to Y’s price, and what relationship does it indicate?
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded of X rises 30/200=15%; Y’s price rises 0.80/8=10%. Cross-price elasticity is 15%/10%=+1.5. The positive sign is consistent with substitution.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, Section P3; latest lecture-based practice variation. Numerical models and diagrams are illustrative, not lecturer measurements.; Notion sample-bank reference: P3.

questions.stem: Price rises from €20 to €24 and quantity demanded falls from 150 to 105 units. Using initial values as the percentage-change bases, what is signed PED and its classification?
questions.explanation: Quantity changes by −45/150=−30%; price changes by 4/20=20%. PED=−30%/20%=−1.5. Its magnitude exceeds one, so demand is elastic over the stated change.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures #6–7 — initial-value elasticity methods; illustrative calculation variation. ; Notion sample-bank reference: M9.

questions.stem: The price of Y rises from €10 to €12 while quantity demanded of X falls from 80 to 72 units, other things equal. Using initial-value percentages, what is X’s cross-price elasticity with respect to Y’s price, and what relationship does it indicate?
questions.explanation: X quantity changes by −8/80=−10%; Y price changes by 2/10=20%. The ratio is −0.5, whose negative sign indicates complements.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures #6–7 — initial-value elasticity methods; illustrative calculation variation. ; Notion sample-bank reference: M10.

questions.stem: Income rises from €2,000 to €2,200 and quantity demanded rises from 50 to 54 units, other things equal. Using initial-value percentages, what is income elasticity and the good’s classification over this change?
questions.explanation: Quantity rises by 4/50=8% and income by 200/2,000=10%, giving +0.8. A positive elasticity identifies a normal good; it does not need to exceed one.
questions.source: EC2204 Lectures #6–7 — initial-value elasticity methods; illustrative calculation variation. ; Notion sample-bank reference: M11.

questions.stem: A supplier cuts price from €20 to €18; sales rise from 100 to 130 units. Using the original price and quantity as the base for percentage changes, which combination is closest?
questions.explanation: The original-base quantity change is +30%, and the price change is −10%, giving PED = −3. Revenue rises from €20 × 100 = €2,000 to €18 × 130 = €2,340.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q9; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q9.

questions.stem: A restaurant raises menu prices by 8%. Quantity demanded falls by 4%, while average variable cost per meal is unchanged. Which statement is defensible?

options.text: Demand is elastic and revenue must fall.
Revenue must fall because demand slopes downward.
Revenue increases approximately, but the effect on profit cannot be established without cost and quantity information.

questions.explanation: Revenue changes by a factor of 1.08 × 0.96 = 1.0368, an increase of 3.68%. Option D is the best available answer because the stem does not hold fixed or other costs constant. If fixed costs were unchanged and unit variable cost were non-negative and unchanged, profit would rise: revenue increases while total variable cost falls. The exact profit change cannot be calculated from the supplied information.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q10; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q10.

questions.stem: The price of Brand A coffee increases by 12%; sales of Brand B coffee rise by 9%; sales of biscuits fall by 6%. Using the simple percentage-change method, which is correct?

options.text: Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is −0.75, suggesting complements.
Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is +0.75, suggesting substitutes.
Own-price elasticity of A is +1.33, implying a Giffen good.
Income elasticity of biscuits is −0.50, suggesting an inferior good.

questions.explanation: The cross-price elasticity of Brand B with respect to Brand A’s price is 9%/12% = +0.75. A positive cross-price elasticity is consistent with substitutes. The biscuit response concerns cross-price, not income, elasticity.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q11; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q11.

questions.stem: A student values successive café lunches at €16, €13, €10 and €7, and each lunch costs €9. Assuming independent marginal values and no other constraints, how many lunches maximise consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: The first three lunches have marginal values above their €9 price, adding €7, €4 and €1 to surplus. The fourth lunch would reduce surplus by €2, so three lunches maximise it.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q13; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q13.

questions.stem: OpenStax's smartphone demand table has point B at P=$70, Q=2,800 and point C at P=$80, Q=2,600. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute PED between B and C?
questions.explanation: Absolute midpoint PED = (200/2700)/(10/75) = 0.5556, approximately 0.56. A value below one means demand is inelastic.

questions.stem: Alarm-clock supply changes from P=$10, Q=80 to P=$11, Q=88. Using midpoint percentages, what is PES?
questions.explanation: Midpoint PES = (8/84)/(1/10.5) = 1. Quantity supplied and price change by the same percentage, so supply is unit elastic.
questions.source: OS6; adapted from OpenStax, Chapter 5, self-check 2 — https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/5-self-check-questions. Principles of Economics 3e, Steven A. questions.stem: A pharmaceutical firm wants to increase revenue from its hair-growth treatment. Demand has an absolute price elasticity of 1.4 at the current price. For a small price change with other conditions unchanged, which recommendation follows?

options.text: Raise price because demand is inelastic.
Lower price because demand is elastic.
Keep price unchanged because demand is unit elastic.
Lower quantity independently of price because revenue is fixed.

questions.explanation: An absolute PED of 1.4 means demand is elastic. For a small price reduction, the percentage quantity increase exceeds the percentage price reduction, raising total revenue.

Greenlaw, David Shapiro and Daniel MacDonald, OpenStax (2022). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/. MCQ options adapted for study.; Notion sample-bank reference: OS7.

questions.stem: Average income rises from $25,000 to $38,000 while annual bread purchases fall from 30 to 22 loaves. Using initial-value percentage changes, which result is correct?

options.text: Income elasticity is about +1.95; bread is normal.
Income elasticity is about −1.95; bread is inferior.
Income elasticity is about +0.51; bread is inferior.
Income elasticity is about −0.51; bread is inferior.

questions.explanation: Using initial values, income elasticity = ((22−30)/30)/((38000−25000)/25000) = −0.5128. The negative sign identifies bread as an inferior good in this example.

questions.stem: The cross-price elasticity of apple demand with respect to the orange price is +0.4. If orange prices fall by 3%, what is the approximate change in apple demand, other things equal?
questions.explanation: Percentage change in apple demand = cross-price elasticity × percentage change in orange price = 0.4 × (−3%) = −1.2%. The positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.

questions.stem: In OpenStax's José example, the budget is $56, a T-shirt costs $14 and a movie costs $7. Which proposed bundle is unaffordable?
questions.explanation: Two T-shirts and five movies cost 2 × $14 + 5 × $7 = $63, exceeding the $56 budget. Each other listed bundle costs $56.

options.text: It stays unchanged because expenditure is unchanged.

questions.explanation: The utility gain from two movies is 31 utils and the lost fourth T-shirt contributes 18 utils. The net change is 31 − 18 = +13 utils.

chapters.description: Questions from EC2204 — Sample MCQs in Notion, grouped by topic. OpenStax adaptations are integrated with the related course questions.

questions.stem: As positive output rises, average fixed cost:
questions.explanation: AFC = FC/Q; an unchanged fixed cost is spread over more units.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 91; Notion sample-bank reference: 91.

questions.stem: If marginal cost is below average total cost, an increase in output causes average total cost to:
questions.explanation: Adding units that cost less than the current average lowers that average.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 96; Notion sample-bank reference: 96.

questions.stem: In perfect competition, why is marginal revenue equal to price for an individual firm?

options.text: The firm is a price taker and can sell additional output at the market price
The firm chooses the market price

questions.explanation: A price-taking firm receives the same market price for an extra unit, so MR = P.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 59; Notion sample-bank reference: 59.

questions.stem: For a perfectly competitive firm that operates in the short run, an interior profit-maximising output on the rising part of MC satisfies:

options.text: Price = marginal cost = average total cost

questions.explanation: P = MR = MC is the output rule, provided operating covers variable costs. Equality with ATC is not required in the short run. The original four options omitted the general correct rule.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 94; Notion sample-bank reference: 94.

questions.stem: A professional leaves a €120,000 salary to start a business. Which cost is most relevant to the economist but may not appear in the firm's accounts?
questions.explanation: The forgone salary is an implicit opportunity cost.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 55; Notion sample-bank reference: 55.

questions.stem: For an audit office, why might a partner's salary be treated differently as a fixed or variable cost?

options.text: Because the classification can depend on the time horizon and how the partner's workload changes with output
Because all salaries are always fixed
Because partner salaries are never costs
Because fixed costs always change with output

questions.explanation: Cost classification depends on the relevant time horizon and whether the expense varies with output.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 56; Notion sample-bank reference: 56.

questions.stem: A firm's total cost rises from €10,000 to €10,600 when output rises from 100 to 120 units. What is the marginal cost per additional unit?
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 57; Notion sample-bank reference: 57.

questions.stem: At the current output, a firm's marginal revenue is €900 and marginal cost is €700. What should the firm do if it wants to increase profit?

options.text: Keep output unchanged because MR is irrelevant

questions.explanation: MR − MC = €900 − €700 = €200 for an additional unit, so expanding output can raise profit.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 58; Notion sample-bank reference: 58.

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. Labour is the only variable input. What wage is paid per worker?

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. When which worker is employed do diminishing marginal returns begin?

questions.stem: Workers / output / variable cost (€): 0/0/0; 1/25/10; 2/55/20; 3/86/30; 4/110/40; 5/130/50; 6/145/60; 7/155/70; 8/160/80. Fixed cost is €150 at every output. The firm is perfectly competitive, market price is €0.50 and fixed costs are unavoidable. Which pair of listed outputs maximises short-run profit?
questions.explanation: At 110: TR = 0.50 × 110 = €55; TC = 150 + 40 = €190; profit = −€135. At 130: TR = €65; TC = €200; profit = −€135. Net revenue TR − VC is €15 at both outputs; other table outputs yield less. Moving from 110 to 130 adds €10 revenue and €10 cost. Both maximise profit;
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 90; Notion sample-bank reference: 90.

questions.stem: When land prices increase from €6,000 to €10,000 per acre but acreage supplied is unchanged, the price elasticity of supply over this change is:
questions.explanation: %ΔQs = 0, so PES = 0: perfectly inelastic supply over the observed range. The original stem asked for a property of supply but offered bare numbers.

questions.stem: According to marginal analysis, optimal decision-making involves:

options.text: Expanding an activity until total benefit is zero
Taking actions whenever marginal benefit is positive
Taking actions only if marginal cost is zero
Taking actions while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost; being indifferent to an increment when they are equal

questions.explanation: Compare additional benefit with additional cost. Equality adds zero net benefit and can produce tied optima.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 95; Notion sample-bank reference: 95.

questions.stem: A business earns €160,000 revenue and pays €100,000 explicit costs. Its owner’s forgone salary is €70,000, the only implicit cost. What are accounting profit and economic profit, respectively?
questions.explanation: Accounting profit = €160,000 − €100,000 = €60,000. Economic profit also deducts the €70,000 forgone salary, giving −€10,000.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M5.

questions.stem: At Q=200, fixed cost is €600 and total variable cost is €1,400. Which set gives AFC, AVC and ATC, respectively?
questions.explanation: AFC=600/200=€3; AVC=1,400/200=€7; ATC=(600+1,400)/200=€10 per unit. Total cost must not be confused with cost per unit.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M12.

questions.stem: With capital fixed, hiring one more worker increases output from 240 to 280 units and total cost from €1,800 to €1,920. What are that worker’s marginal product and the marginal cost per extra output unit over this interval?
questions.explanation: The worker adds 280−240=40 units. The additional cost is €120, so marginal cost over this batch is €120/40=€3 per unit.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M13.

questions.stem: A price-taking firm can produce Q=0, 1, 2 or 3 units. Total costs are €50, €62, €80 and €106, respectively. Price is €20 per unit and the €50 fixed cost is unavoidable. Which listed output maximises short-run profit?
questions.explanation: Profits at Q=0,1,2,3 are −€50, −€42, −€40 and −€46. Q=2 yields the smallest loss and therefore the highest profit; producing nothing still incurs fixed cost.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #8 — costs, marginal product and output choice; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M14.

questions.stem: A Cork food producer increases the price received per unit from €10 to €14. Quantity supplied rises from 80 to 110 units per week. Using the original price and quantity as the base for percentage changes, what is the price elasticity of supply (PES), and how should it be classified?
questions.explanation: Using original values, percentage quantity change is 30/80 = 37.5% and percentage price change is 4/10 = 40%. PES = 37.5%/40% = 0.9375 ≈ 0.94, which is inelastic because it is below one.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q19; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q19.

questions.stem: The figure shows a price-taking firm with P=MR=€14. Using its marginal cost curve, which output maximises short-run profit (assuming the firm operates)?
questions.explanation: For an operating price-taking firm, the profit-maximising output is where rising MC equals P = MR. In the graph MC meets €14 at Q = 20. AVC is below price there, so operating is consistent with the stated assumption even though ATC is above price.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q14; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q14.

questions.stem: A bakery’s total cost rises from €1,200 at 100 loaves to €1,260 at 110 loaves. Average total cost at 100 loaves is €12. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Average total cost at 110 loaves must exceed €12.
Marginal cost over the extra ten loaves is €6 per loaf, below initial ATC, so ATC falls over that range.
Marginal cost is €60 per loaf, above ATC.

questions.explanation: The additional ten loaves cost €60, so marginal cost over that range is €60/10 = €6 per loaf. This is below initial ATC of €12. New ATC is €1,260/110 ≈ €11.45, which is lower.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q15; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q15.

questions.stem: Is it possible for accounting profit to be positive and economic profit to be negative?

options.text: No, accounting and economic profit are identical.
Yes, when total explicit and implicit opportunity costs exceed revenue even though explicit costs alone do not.
No, economic profit must always exceed accounting profit.
Yes, simply because fixed costs are a small proportion of total costs.

questions.explanation: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs. Economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 93; Answers independently derived where the Notion source is answer-free.; Notion sample-bank reference: 93.

questions.stem: A firm earns $1,000,000 revenue and incurs explicit costs of $600,000 labour, $150,000 capital and $200,000 materials. Its own land could earn $30,000 annual rent elsewhere. What are accounting profit and economic profit respectively?
questions.explanation: Explicit costs total $950,000, so accounting profit is $1,000,000 − $950,000 = $50,000. Deducting the $30,000 forgone rent gives economic profit of $20,000.

questions.stem: Assume a bakery is a price taker in a perfectly competitive bread market. Market demand slopes down; the bakery has fixed costs and rising marginal cost. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakery can ensure that its price exceeds average cost.
The bakery faces a flat demand curve at the market price.
The bakery’s supply curve is horizontal.
The bakery always earns positive economic rent.

questions.explanation: The firm can sell at the given market price, so its own demand is horizontal. Merely having many bakeries would not establish price-taking without the added assumption.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, question 97; Notion sample-bank reference: 97.

questions.stem: A water network has high fixed costs and low marginal costs, making one supplier cheaper than duplicated networks. Which concept describes this?
questions.explanation: One firm can serve the relevant market at lower total cost.

questions.stem: Many differentiated sellers can enter a monopolistically competitive market. Incumbents initially earn positive economic profit. The diagram illustrates the eventual equilibrium. Which adjustment best explains it?

options.text: Entry expands each incumbent’s demand until economic profit keeps rising.
Entry reduces each incumbent’s demand until demand/AR is tangent to AC and economic profit is zero.
Entry necessarily removes differentiation and places every firm at minimum AC.
Positive economic profit acts as a legal barrier preventing entry.

questions.explanation: Entry divides demand among more sellers. The standard long-run outcome has P=AC at demand–AC tangency and MR=MC at the chosen output. It is not generally at minimum AC. The illustrative curves meet these conditions at Q=30.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, Section O, medium-priority variation 2; latest lecture-based practice variation. Numerical models and diagrams are illustrative, not lecturer measurements.; Notion sample-bank reference: O5.

options.text: Perfect competition; firms face horizontal demand and ignore rival responses.
Monopoly; a single seller faces no existing rivals.
Monopolistic competition; many small sellers face easy entry.

questions.explanation: A few important firms, difficult entry and attention to rival reactions fit oligopoly and strategic interdependence. Product differentiation does not rule out oligopoly.

Increase output because extra units cost less than the price received.

questions.stem: A single-price monopolist faces P=100−Q and MR=100−2Q. It has already selected Q=30. Using the diagram, which curve and price identify what customers will pay?

options.text: MR at Q=30, giving €40 per unit.
Demand/AR at Q=30, giving €70 per unit.
MC at Q=30, giving €20 per unit.
Demand/AR at Q=40, giving €60 per unit.

questions.explanation: Price is read from demand/AR at the selected output: 100−30=€70. MR at the same quantity is €40, not the selling price. The question takes Q=30 as given; it is not asking for the optimum under the illustrated MC.

questions.stem: The diagram compares monopoly (Q=40, P=€60) with a competitive benchmark (Q=80, P=€20), using the same demand and marginal cost. What do the shaded regions A and B represent?

options.text: A is deadweight loss; B is a transfer to the producer.
Both A and B are additional fixed costs.
A is a transfer from consumers to the producer; B is deadweight loss.
Both A and B are consumer surplus retained after monopoly pricing.

questions.explanation: A represents extra payment on the units still traded, transferred from consumers to the producer. B is the net benefit of units between Q=40 and Q=80 that are no longer traded. A transfer changes who receives surplus; B is a loss of total surplus.

questions.stem: Why might a government grant patent protection even though the resulting market power can create deadweight loss?

options.text: It guarantees that the protected firm sets price equal to marginal cost.
It removes the resources needed for research and development.
It makes consumer surplus equal to producer surplus.
The prospect of protected returns can encourage innovation, creating a trade-off with restricted output.

questions.explanation: Patent protection can support incentives to innovate while permitting market power and forgone beneficial trades. The rationale is a trade-off, not a claim that monopoly has no welfare cost.
questions.source: EC2204 — Sample MCQs, Section O, high-priority variation 3; latest lecture-based practice variation. Numerical models and diagrams are illustrative, not lecturer measurements.; Notion sample-bank reference: O3.

questions.stem: A single-price monopolist faces inverse demand P=120−2Q. Which pair correctly gives its total-revenue and marginal-revenue functions in the continuous linear model?
questions.explanation: TR=P×Q=120Q−2Q². Differentiating TR gives MR=120−4Q. For linear demand the MR slope is twice the demand slope.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #10 — linear demand, TR, MR and price; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M15.

questions.stem: A single-price monopolist has P=120−2Q, MR=120−4Q and constant MC=€40. Assume it operates, can choose continuous output and has no capacity constraint. What output and selling price maximise profit?
questions.explanation: MR=MC gives 120−4Q=40, so Q=20. The price comes from demand: P=120−2(20)=€80, not from the MR curve.
questions.source: EC2204 Lecture #10 — linear demand, TR, MR and price; illustrative calculation variation. Notion sample-bank reference: M16.

questions.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost MC = 20 + 0.5Q. Which output–price pair maximises profit?
questions.explanation: TR = (100 − 2Q)Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. Equating MR with MC gives 100 − 4Q = 20 + 0.5Q, hence Q = 80/4.5 ≈ 17.78. Price is read from demand: P = 100 − 2(17.78) ≈ €64.44. Rounded, this is Q ≈ 18 and P ≈ €64.

questions.stem: Two supermarket chains repeatedly compete in a small town. Each has an incentive to discount if the rival maintains its price, but both would earn more if neither discounted. Which explanation is strongest?

options.text: Monopolistic competition: strategic interaction is impossible.
Natural monopoly: one firm must have falling average cost at every output.
Perfect competition: each chain is necessarily a price taker.
An oligopoly prisoner’s dilemma: individually attractive discounting can leave both worse off.

questions.explanation: The two chains are strategically interdependent. Each has an individual incentive to discount, although mutual restraint would make both better off. This is the incentive conflict in an oligopoly prisoner’s dilemma.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q17; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q17.

questions.stem: A patented pharmaceutical product faces an approaching patent expiry, powerful hospital purchasing groups and a high-cost regulatory approval process for new entrants. Which combination best describes Porter’s forces?

options.text: Buyer power is high; threat of entry is constrained by regulation, while the patent expiry may intensify rivalry or substitutes.
Threat of entry is automatically high because regulation is costly.
Buyer power is necessarily low because hospitals are large.

questions.explanation: Powerful purchasing groups indicate high buyer power. Costly regulatory approval constrains entry. Patent expiry can expose the product to stronger competition, especially generic entry and subsequent rivalry; it does not eliminate rivalry. The precise substitute classification depends on the industry boundary.
questions.source: Sample+2204+MCQ.docx, Q18; answers independently derived, not a supplied official key.; Notion sample-bank reference: Q18.
